result.reason: Letter A is clearer: it establishes date, strategy, both account numbers, the period, and the basis of the figures before presenting results, then defines the jargon a lay reader would trip on (net vs. gross as "what you actually earned after our advisory fee"; 11.2x vs 13.6x forward earnings as "a lower price per dollar of expected earnings"). Its fee paragraph moves in a single logical sequence from tiers to asset level to effective date to proration. Letter B is muddier: the sentence about regional banks "cutting their yields" from 12.0% to 8.5% reads as something the banks did rather than a portfolio action, leaving an untrained reader unsure what changed; it carries no date or account identifiers; and it leans on unverifiable phrases ("strong long-term potential," "provides a cushion against future volatility"). On tone, the notes describe a direct, numbers-first client with two specific questions, and A answers both explicitly — the portfolio "gave up less ground than the index," and the fee "will be lower from August 1 onward than it would have been under the prior schedule" — closing briskly with an invitation to call. B softens exactly where this client wants precision: it omits the $6,420,000 asset figure in favor of "reached $5,000,000," drops the year-to-date and trailing three-year returns, and adds generic relationship warmth and promotional register ("benefit from," "continued trust in our partnership") better suited to a deferential client than to one who took over the relationship and wants the numbers. The preference is not driven by length; A is stronger sentence by sentence and at each point where the tone notes set an expectation.
